Green Gentrification in Glasgow¶

March 2025¶

Introduction¶

City planners increasingly acknowledge that urban greening plays a crucial role in enhancing cities' social and environmental sustainability (Du & Zhang, 2020). However, planners must be careful when implementing their urban greening plans, as poorly designed plans may lead to green gentrification in the future (Anguelovski et al., 2022). Green gentrification refers to the displacement of marginalized people from areas near urban greenspaces due to an influx of wealthier residents (Barcelona Lab for Urban Environmental Justice and Sustainability, n.d.).

However, most research focuses on green gentrification resulting from newly developed urban greenspaces. Many cities worldwide, particularly in the UK, are experiencing critical housing shortages (Barton et al., 2023; UNISON Scotland, 2016). These shortages create an urban landscape where limited housing stock can lead to rapid rent increases, enabling wealthier residents to afford more desirable locations, such as urban greenspaces, thus displacing deprived residents.

The housing market dynamics have been further complicated by changes in housing policy and the lack of affordable housing following the 2008 global financial crisis. Therefore, the burden of housing has increasingly fallen onto the private rental sector. This shift has resulted in a significant increase in privately rented households, with marginalised people disproportionately renting from private landlords (Bailey, 2020). Without adequate rent controls, private landlords can increase rents with little pushback from marginalised people.

Thus, by focusing on the private rental sector, this study aims to gain insight into Glasgow’s (Scotland) property market. Here we leverage property listings from Zoopla (Zoopla HomeTrack, 2023) (with access from the UBDC) as well as open mapping data from the Ordnance Survey (n.d.), and deprivation data from the Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation (SIMD) from the Scottish Government (2020) to analyse spatial and temporal trends in private rents to find whether green gentrification is taking place in Glasgow.

Data and Methods¶

Data Overview¶

Unlike traditional housing studies relying on Census data captured every 5-10 years, this research benefits from utilising private rental listings from Zoopla to analyse short-term housing market volatility (Begum, 2021). Boeing and Waddell (2017) have demonstrated that online property listings from Craigslist have provided effective real-time trend monitoring. Moreover, the Zoopla data has shown to be robust for rental market analysis (Livingston, 2021; Bailey, 2025). The private rental listings were accessed under an end-user licence from the Urban Big Data Centre (UBDC), licensed from Zoopla Plc (Zoopla HomeTrack, 2023).

The Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation (SIMD) provides neighborhood deprivation scores through deciles, with 1 representing the most deprived 10% and 10 the least deprived 10% (Scottish Government, 2020). This composite index incorporates income, health, employment, education, housing, crime, and service access data. By tracking these scores, we can track whether neighbourhoods are becoming more or less deprived over time. The Scottish Government releases SIMD data at the datazone level, with each zone comprising 500-1000 people. Therefore, a datazone in this study implies a neighbourhood.

Spatial analysis utilises maps from the Ordnance Survey (n.d.) to visualise greenspaces and datazone boundaries, sourced from open data provided by the Scottish Government (n.d.).

Methodology¶

The analysis here followed several key steps. Firstly, rental listings data from Zoopla and SIMD are read and merged using Pandas. The dataset is then cleaned by removing outliers and focusing on flats only. Next, Principal Components Analysis (PCA) is performed on rent price and SIMD decile to create indices for 2016 and 2024. Finally, a K-Means Clustering model is utilised to identify patterns in Glasgow's rental market.

Note that the rental prices used in this analysis are the "price of the property which appeared on the last day of the listing life" (Zoopla HomeTrack, 2023).

Data Cleaning:¶

The first step to clean the dataset is to remove outliers. The minimum and maximum weekly rental prices are £17 and £28,845 (GBP Sterling), respectively. These seem unreasonable, but a histogram of rental prices is visualised to inspect this further.

In [13]:
print("Minimum Rent Price = (GBP) £", min(glasgow_dataset['price']))
print("Maximum Rent Price = (GBP) £", max(glasgow_dataset['price']))

# View the histogram of rental prices:
sns.histplot(glasgow_dataset['price'], kde=True)
plt.ylabel('Frequency')
plt.xlabel('Rental Price per week (GBP £)')
plt.title('Rent Price distribution', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.show()

Minimum Rent Price = (GBP) £ 17
Maximum Rent Price = (GBP) £ 28845

The histogram clearly shows that a maximum weekly rent price of £28,845 is far too high. Thus, the dataset is filtered such that only listings between £50 (lower bound) and £400 (upper bound) per week are kept. Now, the price distribution looks much better and captures higher rent values sufficiently whilst minimising the inclusion of extreme prices.

In [15]:

glasgow_dataset = glasgow_dataset.loc[(glasgow_dataset['price'] > 50) & (glasgow_dataset['price'] < 400)]

plt.ylabel('Frequency')
plt.xlabel('Rental Price per week (GBP £)')

plt.show()

<Figure size 1500x800 with 0 Axes>

The boxplots show the distribution of weekly rental prices across SIMD deciles in 2016 and 2020, by year, and by number of bedrooms.

As the SIMD decile increases - implying less deprivation - greater weekly rental prices become less extreme, as shown by the fewer outliers for SIMD scores of 8, 9, and 10. This means in less deprived areas, expensive flats are more common, and more people can afford to live in them. Whereas, in neighbourhoods with higher deprivation (SIMD scores 1-7), variability in rent price is greater, with more outliers for more expensive rents. Similarly, looking at the distribution of rental prices per year, rents are increasing over time, with higher-priced rentals becoming more common. Listings with more than 6 bedrooms were excluded from the dataset, as rent prices become more random for flats with more than 6 bedrooms.

Data Analysis¶

Now, the spatial and temporal trends of rental properties in Glasgow can be investigated. Beginning with the spatial patterns, a scatter plot of the rent price is plotted on top of a map of the urban greenspaces in Glasgow. Only public parks or gardens are plotted

In [24]:
# Load urban greenspace data using geopandas.
greenspaces = gpd.read_file("GreenspaceData/NS_GreenspaceSite.shp")
function_types = ['Public Park Or Garden']
greenspaces = greenspaces[greenspaces['function'].isin(function_types)]
greenspaces = greenspaces.to_crs(epsg=4326)

# Only include data within the Glasgow area such that the map is centred on Glasgow.
glasgow_box = {"xmin": -4.433,"ymin": 55.789,"xmax": -4.081,"ymax": 55.953}
glasgow_greenspaces = greenspaces.cx[glasgow_box["xmin"]:glasgow_box["xmax"],glasgow_box["ymin"]:glasgow_box["ymax"]].to_crs(epsg=3857)

From the scatter plot above, it is clear that the majority of the highest prices, yellow points, are paid in Glasgow's West End. Central and south Glasgow also show expensive prices, but far less than the West End.

Next, the temporal trends of rental prices are visualised. The figure below shows the median weekly rent price for each SIMD decile and each year:

# Take SIMD Deciles, year, and price values, then pivot the dataframe such that SIMD Decile are the columns with price populating the dataframe values.
time_series_2016 = glasgow_dataset.groupby(["SIMD2016_Decile", "year"], as_index=False).agg({"price": "median"})
time_series_2016 = time_series_2016.pivot(index = "year", columns = ["SIMD2016_Decile"], values = "price")

time_series_2024 = glasgow_dataset.groupby(["SIMD2020_Decile", "year"], as_index=False).agg({"price": "median"})
time_series_2024 = time_series_2024.pivot(index = "year", columns = ["SIMD2020_Decile"], values = "price")

# Separate out the data for years 2016 - 2019 for SIMD 2016 data, and 2020 - 2024 for SIMD 2020 data.
time_series_2016 = time_series_2016.filter(items=[2016, 2017, 2018, 2019], axis=0)
time_series_2024 = time_series_2024.filter(items=[2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024], axis=0)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=(12, 8), sharey = True)

The charts above show that between 2016 to 2019, the median weekly rental prices in Glasgow remained relatively stable. Over this period, the weekly median rent increased by 11% for the most deprived populations (SIMD = 1). Whereas, from 2020 to 2024, rents increased steeply. For the most deprived populations, rents increased by 43%, which could be an impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Surprisingly, rents for the least deprived populations (SIMD = 9 or 10) decrease from 2023 to 2024. Collectively, these two groups saw a decrease of 4.7% from 2023 to 2024. Whilst this is not substantial, should the trend continue, it will warrant further analysis.

Principal Components Analysis¶

Rental price and SIMD data are now combined to form a single index via Principal Components Analysis (PCA). Two PCA indices are created, one for 2016 and another for 2024. The 2016 index incorporates average median weekly rent prices for 2016-2019 with the 2016 SIMD decile scores. Similarly, the 2024 index combines average median weekly rental prices for 2020-2024 with the 2020 SIMD decile scores.

The difference in these two indices is used to fit a K-means clustering model to group datazones into distinct categories for spatial analysis.

Note that since the Zoopla rental listings data does not contain information for each datazone in Glasgow, some datazones are lost. So, the following analysis is applicable for 616 out of 746 datazones in Glasgow (Scottish Government, no date). Nonetheless, 82% of datazones are retained, which should be sufficient to form reliable judgements.

In [31]:
# Form the master dataset for PCA - group by datazone, SIMD deciles, and year, and populate the rows with median weekly rent price.
pca_dataset = glasgow_dataset.groupby(["datazone", "SIMD2016_Decile","SIMD2020_Decile", "year"], as_index=False).agg({"price": "median"})
pca_dataset = pca_dataset.pivot(index=["datazone", "SIMD2016_Decile", "SIMD2020_Decile"], columns="year", values="price")

# Reset index
pca_dataset.reset_index(inplace=True)

# Remove index name
pca_dataset.columns.name = None
pca_dataset.head()

# Calculate the average median weekly rental price for 2 sets of data - 2016-2019 - which includes data for 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2019. 
# And 2020-2024 - which includes data for 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024.
pca_dataset.loc[:, "average_price_2016-2019"] = pca_dataset.loc[:, [2016, 2017, 2018,2019]].mean(axis=1)
pca_dataset.loc[:, "average_price_2020-2024"] = pca_dataset.loc[:, [2020, 2021, 2022,2023, 2024]].mean(axis=1)

One problem that occurs is that null values exist for the average median weekly rental price. These null values should not be deleted as they make up over a sixth of the dataset; deleting them would further reduce the number of datazones, decreasing the validity of the study. Thus, the null values are filled using the average price for each SIMD Decile. For example, if a null value exists for a datazone with a 2016 SIMD decile of 1, then the average rental price for an SIMD decile of 1 is used to replace the null value.

In [36]:
# Compute average price per 2016 and 2020 SIMD scores, respectively.
decile_avg_2016 = pca_dataset_2016.groupby("SIMD2016_Decile")["average_price_2016-2019"].transform("mean")
decile_avg_2024 = pca_dataset_2024.groupby("SIMD2020_Decile")["average_price_2020-2024"].transform("mean")

# Fill NAs will the average price per SIMD decile.
pca_dataset_2016.loc[:,"average_price_2016-2019"] = pca_dataset_2016["average_price_2016-2019"].fillna(decile_avg_2016)
pca_dataset_2024.loc[:,"average_price_2020-2024"] = pca_dataset_2024["average_price_2020-2024"].fillna(decile_avg_2024)

Form PCA Indices¶

Before the PCA indices can be formed, the data needs to be standardised and the number of principal components needs to be determined. The StandardScalar and decomposition module from the Sklearn Python Library are utilised to scale the data and find the number of principal components, respectively.

In [39]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn import decomposition 

# Split data from the master dataset into 2016-2019 and 2020-2024 datasets and then normalise with StandardScalar.
data_2016 = pca_dataset_2016[['SIMD2016_Decile', 'average_price_2016-2019']]
scaled_2016 = data_2016.values
scaled_2016 = StandardScaler().fit_transform(scaled_2016)

data_2024 = pca_dataset_2024[['SIMD2020_Decile', 'average_price_2020-2024']]
scaled_2024 = data_2024.values
scaled_2024 = StandardScaler().fit_transform(scaled_2024)

# Convert standardised values into a dataframe.
scaled_2016 = pd.DataFrame(scaled_2016, columns=list(data_2016.columns) ,index=data_2016.index)
scaled_2016.rename(columns = {'SIMD2016_Decile': 'SIMD2016_Decile_norm','average_price_2016-2019': 'average_price_2016-2019_norm'}, inplace = True)
scaled_2016.head()

# Convert standardised values into a dataframe.
scaled_2024 = pd.DataFrame(scaled_2024, columns=list(data_2024.columns), index=data_2024.index)
scaled_2024.rename(columns = {'SIMD2020_Decile': 'SIMD2020_Decile_norm','average_price_2020-2024': 'average_price_2020-2024_norm'}, inplace = True)
scaled_2024.head()

Now that the data is standardised, the optimal number of components should be found such that it maximises the variance explained by each feature. The bar chart below shows that the first principal component offers the best fit for PCA as it captures the greatest variance in the features.

Subsequently, the number of components is set to one for the PCA fits. The PCA module from the Sklearn Python Library is used to calculate the PCA indices.

In [41]:

pca_all.fit(scaled_all)

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
# Using the first principal component, form the PCA indices for 2016 and 2024.

# 2016:
pca_2016 = PCA(n_components=1)
principalComponents_2016 = pca_2016.fit_transform(scaled_2016)
principal_df_2016 = pd.DataFrame(data = principalComponents_2016, columns = ['index_2016'],index=data_2016.index)

# 2024:
pca_2024 = PCA(n_components=1)
principalComponents_2024 = pca_2024.fit_transform(scaled_2024)
principal_df_2024 = pd.DataFrame(data = principalComponents_2024, columns = ['index_2024'],index=data_2016.index)
In [43]:
# Create a dataframe that contains the normalised values of each variable as well as the PCA indices for 2016 and 2024.
# Then, merge these dataframes with the untransformed data (before normalisation) to form a dataset that can be used for cross-analysis.

#2016
df_2016 = pd.concat([principal_df_2016, scaled_2016], axis = 1)
df_2016 = df_2016[['SIMD2016_Decile_norm', "average_price_2016-2019_norm", "index_2016"]]

#2024

df_2024 = df_2024[['SIMD2020_Decile_norm', "average_price_2020-2024_norm", "index_2024"]]

# Combine 2016 and 2024 data in one dataframe.
df_pca_all = df_2016.merge(df_2024, left_index=True, right_index=True, how="inner")

Visualising PCA Indices¶

After calculating the PCA indices, the difference in index from 2024 to 2016 is calculated and stored as index_chg. This variable will be used for analysis and the cluster model.

The principal components data is merged with a GeoDataFrame of Glasgow's datazone boundaries to form a GeoDataFrame that can be used to visualise changes in deprivation and rental prices for each datazone.

In [45]:
# Form dataframe that will be used for the K-means cluster model.

model_df = model_df[["SIMD2016_Decile","average_price_2016-2019","SIMD2016_Decile_norm", "average_price_2016-2019_norm", "index_2016",
          "SIMD2020_Decile","average_price_2020-2024","SIMD2020_Decile_norm","average_price_2020-2024_norm","index_2024"]]

The choropleth map shown above shows the change in PCA index from 2016 to 2024 for each datazone in Glasgow, with public parks and gardens also plotted. Where an area is yellow or orange, the deprivation has decreased, and the average median weekly rent price has increased. Such areas seem to be scattered on the outskirts in the north of the city, whilst in the south, yellow areas are much more tightly clustered together. In both the north and south of Glasgow, yellow datazones are located close to public parks, such as Pollok Country Park, Cowlairs Park, and Springburn Park.

However, we can see that for most datazones, there is little change from 2016 to 2024. This is especially true for north Glasgow. Nonetheless, the datazones can be categorised into discrete groups based on the change in their index value from 2016 to 2024 through a K-means clustering model.

K-Means Clustering Model¶

For the cluster analysis, K-Means is used from the Sklearn Python library. Firstly, the number of clusters in the K-means model must be specified. The Elbow method is used to determine the number of clusters for the model. The following plot shows the within-cluster sum of squares error per number of clusters for 13 models.

From the plot, the elbow appears to be located at K = 4 clusters. Thus, the K-means clustering model is fit with 4 clusters in this analysis.

In [50]:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
import yellowbrick
from yellowbrick.cluster.elbow import kelbow_visualizer
os.environ["OMP_NUM_THREADS"] = "3"

# Extract PCA index change values from the modelling dataframe and and store as a separate dataframe and KMeans requires a dataframe input.
index_chg_df = pd.DataFrame(data = model_df, columns = ['index_chg'])
index_chg_df.index=model_df['DataZone']

# Calculate the error associated with each cluster.
cluster_error = []
for i in range (2,15):
    kclusters = KMeans(n_clusters = i, init = "k-means++", random_state = 12)
    kclusters.fit(index_chg_df)
    cluster_error.append(kclusters.inertia_)

# Create a plot of cluster errors with the associated number of clusters used in the model.
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8), dpi=100)
plt.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)

plt.plot(range(2, 15), cluster_error, marker='o', markersize=10, 
         linewidth=2.5, color='#FFc000',markerfacecolor='white', markeredgewidth=2)

# Title and Axes.
plt.title('K-Means Clustering Error by Number of Clusters', fontsize=18, pad=20, fontweight = 'bold')
plt.xlabel("Number of Clusters", fontsize=14, labelpad=10)
plt.ylabel("Error", fontsize=14, labelpad=10)
plt.xticks(range(2, 15), fontsize=12)
plt.yticks(fontsize=12)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

What do the clusters mean?¶

The table presented below categorizes the average SIMD score and the average rent for 2016 and 2024, for each cluster, respectively. Deprivation scores remain relatively stable over the period. Rents, however, fluctuate at varying degrees. Therefore, the four clusters identified by the K-means model can be explained as:

  • Cluster 0: Relatively stable areas. Even though weekly rent has increased by 17.64%, this is far below the increase observed in national statistics - an 81.8% increase for a two-bedroom flat from 2010 - 2024 (Scottish Government, 2024).
  • Cluster 1: Rapidly increasing rental prices - rents have increased faster than national statistics - 89.16% increase compared to 81.8% (Scottish Government, 2024). These neighbourhoods are most prone to gentrification.
  • Cluster 2: Decreasing rental prices in previously expensive areas. These areas were the most expensive and least deprived areas to rent in 2016. In 2024, rental prices have decreased and deprivation has increased.
  • Cluster 3: Slowly increasing rents.

Therefore, it is cluster 1 that should be focused on as these neighbourhoods are most likely to be susceptible to gentrification. Also, areas categorised under cluster 2 could be declining due to falling rental prices and increasing deprivation. Out of the 616 datazones that have been analysed, 39 have been identified under cluster 1, and 57 are identifiable under cluster 2.

Referring back to the choropleth map of the clusters, above, it is clear that most datazones remain stable (cluster 2), or slowly growing in terms of rent price (cluster 0). Rapidly ascending areas, cluster are more common in south Glasgow than north Glasgow, and only 2 such areas located in east Glasgow. Conversely, neighbourhoods that may be prone to declining - cluster - are more common in north Glasgow.

Putting this together, the South appears to be becoming increasingly more desirable to live in, explaining the rapid increase in rental prices in this area. This implies people are more willing to pay premium prices to live here. Moreover, many ascending areas are located near Glasgow's greenspaces. For example, large public parks such as Pollok Country Park, Cowlairs Park, Sighthill Park, and Springburn Park are surrounded by neighbourhoods where rents have rapidly increased. Moreover, Cuningar Woodland Park, Bellahouston Park, Newlands Park, and Maryhill Park are all located near such neighbourhoods as well. However, population churn data, we can not identify, for certain, if people moving into cluster 2 neighbourhoods around greenspaces are wealthier and displacing less affluent populations. But, given that rents have been rapidly increasing in these datazones, we can say that areas surrounding and near large public parks are urban hotspots that are more desirable to live in and may attract wealthier residents, which makes these neighbourhoods more susceptible to gentrification.

Evaluation¶

To assess the quality of the clusters, the silhouette score and Calinski-Harabasz Score are used to quantify the goodness of fit for the K-means clustering model.

The following graph records the silhouette scores for various values of K. A higher score suggests the data points are well-matched to their respective cluster, implying a good clustering structure. From the plot, below, it is clear that the optimal number of clusters was four, as selected in the final model. Furthermore, the high Calinski Harabasz Score, see below, shows the clusters are compact and well separated from each other, indicating a well-fit K-means cluster model.

However, one problem with the analysis is that we can not say with any degree of certainty that certain areas are actually gentrifying. Without information on population churn for each datazone, there is no way to definitively prove whether wealthier residents are moving into neighbourhoods where rents have increased massively, thereby displacing less affluent residents who can no longer afford to live in that area. Also, the deprivation statistic used in this study, the SIMD decile, changes very little from 2016 to 2024; this means the PCA index and K-means model are more sensitive to changes in rent prices as these fluctuate more readily.

In [59]:
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# Initialise K values and silhouette scores.
k_values = range(2, 15)
silhouette_scores = []

# Calculate scores for each model with K clusters.
for k in k_values:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++', n_init=10, max_iter=100, random_state=42)
    km.fit(index_chg_df)
    
    # Calculate the average silhouette score
    silhouette_avg = silhouette_score(index_chg_df, km.labels_)  
    silhouette_scores.append(silhouette_avg)
    
# Create a plot to visualize Silhouette Scores

Conclusion¶

It is clear from the findings that the data enables a good K-means model to be produced with meaningful categories that can be explored in more detail.

The clusters produced by the model show that most areas in Glasgow are stable or rents are slightly increasing. Some neighbourhoods have experienced exponential increases in rent prices, which are more susceptible to gentrification. Many of these neighbourhoods are located near large public greenspaces - which implies urban greenspaces are highly desirable locations, making areas around public parks more vulnerable to gentrification.

The private rental listings from Zoopla Plc used here have proven to be extremely robust for studying trends in Glasgow's rental market. The fine-grained geographical data allowed for deep spatial analysis, helping to identify hotspots where rents have changed significantly. Also, the data allowed us to observe real-time changes in the markets and identify possible explanations for these rapid fluctuations. For example, the time-series plots show that rents jumped up massively from 2020, showing the impact COVID-19 has had on the property market (Gamber et al., 2023; Kmetz et al., 2022).

However, the model produced in this study is highly sensitive to fluctuations in rent prices. Incorporating datazone-level socio-economic data, such as income, employment, and education, would offer more nuance than a single composite deprivation index. Therefore, we could not find definitive evidence that marginalised people are being displaced from areas near urban greenspaces, leading to green gentrification in Glasgow.

Nonetheless, the analysis has enabled neighbourhoods to be categorised into distinct clusters, allowing areas to be identified as more susceptible to gentrification or at risk of decline. City planners can use this analysis to monitor at-risk neighbourhoods in order to minimise the risk of displacement for less affluent residents. They could also track real-time changes in the rental market to introduce rent control measures when rent prices skyrocket, ensuring residents are protected from market pressures.

import io
import os
from nbformat import current

total_markdown = 0
total_heading = 0
total_code = 0

for root, dirs, files in os.walk("."):
    for file in files:
        if file.endswith(".ipynb") and not file.endswith("checkpoint.ipynb") :
            print(os.path.join(root, file))
            with io.open(os.path.join(root, file), 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
                nb = current.read(f, 'json')

            word_count_markdown = 0
            word_count_heading = 0
            word_count_code = 0
            for cell in nb.worksheets[0].cells:
                if cell.cell_type == "markdown":
                    word_count_markdown += len(cell['source'].replace('#', '').lstrip().split(' '))
                elif cell.cell_type == "heading":
                    word_count_heading += len(cell['source'].replace('#', '').lstrip().split(' '))
                elif cell.cell_type == "code":
                    word_count_code += len(cell['input'].replace('#', '').lstrip().split(' '))
            total_markdown += word_count_markdown
            total_heading += word_count_heading
            total_code += word_count_code
            print("{} Words in notebooks' markdown" .format(word_count_markdown))
            print("{} Words in notebooks' heading" .format(word_count_heading))
            print("{} Words in notebooks' code" .format(word_count_code))
            print("")
